# Stones, generated by rule

T434. The stone, and three things that only showed up when it was
photographed somewhere other than where it was built.

Run it: `UnrealEditor.exe client/Ledger.uproject -game -nearfield`, which now
takes two shots — eye height along the ground, and straight down from eight
metres. `-noscatter` places nothing, which is the control arm.

## What was there before

The scatter was placing `SM_Tree_A` — the settlement's eighteen-metre cone —
because until this task no other mesh existed. The code that did it said so:

> The same two trees the settlement plants, for now. Scatter wants its own rocks
> and shrubs … until those meshes exist, borrowing these is honest about what is
> placed and lets the placement itself be measured.

Honest, and much worse than it sounded. Two things compounded it. The instance
scale was `0.75 + u * 0.7`, chosen when the mesh was a tree, so every instance
was a full-sized tree — the eye-height capture was a dense black forest two
kilometres from the town, and that forest was what made a fifth of that frame
pure black (see `docs/comparisons/sky-light/`). And `Instance.Variant` was
masked to one bit, so a third mesh could never have been placed even once it
existed.

## The stone

`LedgerRock::Describe` — an icosahedron subdivided twice to 320 faces,
displaced radially by two bands of noise, squashed towards its poles because a
stone at rest is wider than it is tall, and lifted so its lowest point is at
zero rather than its centre.

Flat shaded, deliberately: every face carries its own three vertices and one
normal. Smooth normals over a displaced sphere give a soft blob that reads as a
potato; a normal per face gives the flat planes and hard edges a broken rock
actually has. `Roundness` runs the high-frequency band from 0.30 down to 0.05,
which is the difference between a fragment that broke off yesterday and a
water-worn cobble — the one axis of variety that reads at the size these are
drawn.

Three of them, baked alongside the ship and the trees:

```
SM_Rock_A           320 tris  nanite off  lods 1  slots 1  collision yes
SM_Rock_B           320 tris  nanite off  lods 1  slots 1  collision yes
SM_Rock_C           320 tris  nanite off  lods 1  slots 1  collision yes
```

### Sizes that sort like a real clast distribution

`0.15 + u² × 0.85`, so half the stones are under 36 cm, one in ten over 70 cm,
none over a metre. Cubed was tried first and put half the field under 22 cm,
which at three metres is not a stone, it is a speckle. A uniform distribution —
what was there — makes every instance the same size, which is the one
distribution real ground never has.

## Tested

`Ledger.Rock.IsSolidAndRoughlyStoneShaped` checks each variant is 320 faces and
960 vertices, is about a metre across, has height (a stone squashed to a card is
exactly the artefact that prompted the test), sits with its base at zero, has no
degenerate faces, is wound front-facing for Unreal, and has outward normals.

**The winding check exists because the first version of this test passed on an
inside-out mesh.** The icosahedron table is the standard right-handed one, whose
faces are counter-clockwise seen from outside; Unreal is left-handed and takes
the opposite winding as front. The normals were outward the whole time, so a
test that only checked normals was satisfied. A normal and a winding are
different claims and the test now makes both.

## Two things T437 found that one photograph had not

Signed off on a single capture of one grassland site, and the four-biome proof
immediately found both.

**The stones were white.** The bake gives each face a warm grey vertex colour
and `M_Flat` is `Tint x VertexColour`, so a white tint should have produced warm
grey stones. It produced white ones, because **an instanced static mesh does not
deliver the mesh's vertex colours to the shader** -- the settlement's two trees
work around exactly this by being two meshes with two materials, and the same
constraint applies here and had not been noticed. Darkening the bake changed
nothing at all, which is what identified it. The colour now lives in the tint
(0.16 linear, which is rock); per-stone variation has to come back some other
way, through per-instance custom data or one material per variant.

**The stones were on a visible lattice.** There has been jitter inside each cell
since the scatter was written, and it is not enough on its own: a cell fills
when a uniform draw falls under the biome's density, so a biome asking for 1.0
fills every cell and jitter inside a full lattice is still a lattice. In the
rainforest that was rows of stones marching in step across a hillside. Capped at
0.55, so nearly half the cells stay empty and the gaps are where the pattern
goes; the sparse biomes this was originally tuned on do not move.

## What is still wrong

Stones band into chains rather than spreading evenly, and **it is not the
collision ring**, which is what this said until T066's visualiser was pointed at
it. `-terrainvis=collision` shows the chains crossing ground that is uniformly
green out to the far mountain, so scatter is allowed everywhere it is banding.
Whatever is lining them up is something else, and the assumption that it was the
ring boundary was written down here twice before a picture disproved it in one
glance.

The black squares that once held this open are resolved: they were a **stale
baked material**. `-bakematerials` after a material change is part of the loop,
and the instances had been drawing with an out-of-date asset. Kept here because
the search for them ruled out four other things first.

The search for those squares ruled out the geometry (the test above), the
winding (flipping it changed their colour, not their shape) and the ground
material (`-noscatter` left clean sand) before finding it, and
`bAffectDistanceFieldLighting = false` on the scatter components cut them from
about fifteen to six along the way and is kept.
